heading: Can't Stay With a Feeling?
after: Further reading: D’Antoni et al., 2022 — Comparative study of EMDR, Brainspotting, and related methods
before_heading: Layer 4: Unstick the Memories You Can Actually Point To
paragraphs: Some people can feel their body just fine, but the moment a real feeling starts coming up in a session, they slide away from it, maybe by explaining it or by agreeing with whatever the therapist says. If that's you, look for a therapist who catches you sliding away and helps you stay with the feeling. A few talk therapies are built to do just that.

In [Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy](https://psykologtidsskriftet.no/debatt/2021/09/intensive-short-term-dynamic-psychotherapy-methods-evidence-indications-and), the therapist points out each slide as it happens and helps you turn back toward the feeling, watching your body for signs of anxiety as you go. Most people who come to this therapy get overwhelmed easily, so they usually get a slower version of it, where the therapist helps them settle whenever the anxiety climbs too high. Then there's [Affect Phobia Therapy](https://psykologtidsskriftet.no/node/15971/pdf), for when one feeling in particular scares you, grief for example: it gets you used to that feeling bit by bit, at a pace your anxiety can handle.

And some people's trouble is with being treated kindly: when someone cares about them, they can't let it in. For them, [Accelerated Experiential Dynamic Psychotherapy](https://www.apa.org/pubs/videos/4310759) first makes sure they don't feel alone with what comes up, then follows how it feels in the body.

As with water therapy, I'd ask before booking: "What do you do when I start moving away from a feeling, and what if I get overwhelmed?" If the answer leaves no room for you to slow down, or to disagree with them about what you're feeling, keep looking.

heading: Imagery Rescripting
after: While EMDR is often treated as a therapy for anyone with trauma
paragraphs: If one scene from your childhood still leaves you feeling helpless, imagery rescripting is a way to go back into it with help. You picture the scene again, and this time somebody steps in to protect you or give you what you needed. At first that's the therapist, and later it's your own adult self. It's close to how I [re-do trauma memories](https://ibogaqueen.substack.com/i/189761959/re-do-trauma-memories) in my inner child guide.

As for whether it works, the best evidence is for adults whose PTSD started in childhood. For them it does about as well as EMDR: in [a trial of 155 of them](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32892758/), both brought symptoms down, and neither came out clearly ahead. You know the new scene is imagined, so it changes how the memory feels without changing what you remember happened. Like EMDR, it takes you back into the memory, so I'd stop whenever it starts to feel like too much, and do some grounding afterward.

heading: Pain That Won't Quit?
after: Inner-child reparenting is another form of integration therapy
before_heading: Optional High-Intensity State-Shift and Release Practices
paragraphs: Maybe pain is what brought you to this guide. If yours has lasted months, and a doctor has checked and found no injury or disease to explain it, two therapies are worth knowing about.

In [Pain Reprocessing Therapy](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8482298), you learn that the pain is a false alarm, your brain signaling danger where there isn't any, partly by paying close attention to how it feels in your body. Then, a little at a time, you go back to things you've been avoiding because of it, like going for walks.

Pain Reprocessing Therapy's first big trial was only in mild to moderate chronic back pain. There, 66% of the people who got four weeks of the therapy rated their pain 0 or 1 out of 10 afterward, compared to 20% of those given a placebo shot, and the gains mostly held a year later.

The second therapy is for pain that seems bound up with stress and feelings about the people in your life. [Emotional Awareness and Expression Therapy](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03918642) works on those feelings directly. Much of the therapy is letting out anger and other feelings you've held back, and rehearsing in role-play what you'd say to someone you've never stood up to.

In a 2024 trial of veterans aged 60 and up, this therapy beat CBT: 63% had their pain drop by at least 30% afterward, compared to 17% with CBT. That's a lower bar than 0 or 1 out of 10, so the two trials' numbers can't be compared.

I haven't found a trial comparing the two. So if your pain seems tied to stress or to people in your life, I'd start with the second, and otherwise with the first. I'd also ask a therapist where they trained in that therapy, and keep track of how it's going the way I describe in the last section, [How I Judge Whether Any of This Is Helping](#§how-i-judge-whether-any-of-this-is-helping).
